title: Maximum power transfer: why a load gets the most power when it matches the source
examples: When does a load get maximum power?
Why is efficiency 50 percent at maximum power?
What load resistance gives maximum power?

explain.say: Why are hi-fi speakers rated at 8 ohms and radio antennas at 50 ohms? Because of matching. On the board, a source is shown as its Thevenin model: 8 volts behind an internal resistance of 4 ohms, feeding a load. We'll vary the load and hunt for the most power.

explain.say: Try a small load, 1 ohm. Lots of current flows, 8 over 5, which is 1.6 amps, but the load's share of the voltage is tiny, so its power, I squared R, is only 2.56 watts. Most of the heat is wasted inside the source. What do you expect with a big load, say 16 ohms?

explain.say: Now the current starves: 8 over 20 is 0.4 amps, so the load gets 0.4 squared times 16, again just 2.56 watts. Too small a load means too little voltage; too big means too little current. Somewhere in between is a peak. Where would you guess it is?

parts.label: Source
parts.ask: Why isn't the power grid matched for maximum power?

parts.label: Load R_L
parts.ask: What is the maximum power transfer theorem?

explain.say: Right at R L equals R th, 4 ohms. The curve on the board is the load power for every load. At 4 ohms, 1 amp flows and the load gets 4 watts, the highest point. In general the peak is V th squared over 4 R th: 64 over 16, which is 4 watts. Is the curve symmetric around its peak?

Not quite, it falls more slowly on the right. And here's the catch: when matched, the source wastes as much as the load gets, so efficiency is only 50 percent. That suits a weak radio signal or a speaker, but never the power grid, which keeps its source resistance far below the loads. Great job! Challenge: what load suits a 6 volt, 2 ohm source?

draw.text: Matched: half the power reaches the load, half heats the source.

faq.q: What is the maximum power transfer theorem?
faq.a: A load draws the most power from a source when the load resistance equals the source's Thevenin resistance. The maximum power is V th squared over four R th.
asks: State the maximum power transfer theorem
When is power to the load maximum?

faq.a: Every real source has some resistance inside it, from its chemistry or its windings. It wastes power as heat and makes the terminal voltage sag under load.
asks: Why does a battery have internal resistance?

faq.q: Why is the efficiency only 50 percent at maximum power?
faq.a: When R L equals R th the same current flows through both, so they get equal power. Half is delivered and half is wasted inside the source.

faq.q: Why isn't the power grid matched for maximum power?
faq.a: The grid needs high efficiency, not the largest possible power from a small source. Its source resistance is kept far smaller than the loads, so very little is wasted.
asks: Do power stations use impedance matching?

faq.a: In audio amplifiers and speakers, radio antennas and their 50 ohm cables, and sensors: wherever a weak signal must deliver as much power as possible.
asks: Real uses of maximum power transfer

facts: At maximum power transfer the efficiency is exactly 50 percent.
Coaxial cables for radio and test equipment are commonly made with a characteristic impedance of 50 ohms.
Moritz von Jacobi described the maximum power idea around 1840, so it is sometimes called Jacobi's law.

quiz.say: A source has a Thevenin voltage of 12 volts and a Thevenin resistance of 3 ohms. What is the most power it can deliver to a load?
quiz.show: A source has V_th = 12 V and R_th = 3 Ω. What is the most power it can deliver to a load?
quiz.why: P max is V th squared over 4 R th: 144 over 12, which is 12 watts, with a 3 ohm load.

wrong.1: That is V squared over R th; the formula divides by four R th.
wrong.2: That divides by two R th; the formula divides by four R th.

quiz.say: What is the efficiency at maximum power transfer?
quiz.show: What is the efficiency at maximum power transfer?
quiz.why: The load and the internal resistance carry the same current and have equal resistance, so they get equal power.

wrong.1: Some power is always lost in the internal resistance.
wrong.2: The load gets half, not a quarter, of the total power.
